intro.html: Two Latin verbs about speech build this family. loqui means to speak; it appears in English as loqu or locu (you may know ventriloquist, “belly speaker”). dicere means to say; it appears as dict (you know predict, “to say before,” and dictionary).

loqu, locut = speak. dict = say. The prefix tells you how: eloquent and elocution (speaking out), colloquial (speaking with others), soliloquy (speaking alone), circumlocution (speaking around the point), interlocutor (speaking between), edict (said out as an order).
One spelling trap: indict is pronounced in-DITE. The c is silent.

words.def: speaking or writing in a fluent, moving way
words.ex: Rosa gave an {eloquent} speech that left the whole gym in tears.
words.ctx: The old fisherman was usually a man of few words, but when the town planned to close the harbor, he became {eloquent}, describing three generations of families who had lived from the sea.
words.etym: From Latin eloquens, “speaking out,” from eloqui: e (out) + loqui (to speak).

mn.text: At graduation, Rosa’s words flow out so gracefully that the grandparents in the front row wipe their eyes. She is {eloquent}.

scene.alt: A graduate gives a moving speech at a podium while a grandmother wipes away happy tears.

words.ex: Our {loquacious} cab driver told us his whole life story before we reached the hotel.
words.ctx: Unlike her quiet twin, Bea was {loquacious}; she could chat for an hour with a stranger at the bus stop and still have more to say.
words.etym: From Latin loquax, “talkative,” from loqui (to speak).

mn.cue: lo-QUACK-cious: a duck who never stops
mn.text: Daisy the duck quacks to everyone she meets, about the weather, the pond, the bread and the weather again. She is {loquacious}.

scene.alt: A chatty duck quacks on and on while a bored frog listens and a turtle falls asleep.

words.ex: “Gonna” is a {colloquial} way of saying “going to.”
words.ctx: The novel’s characters speak in a {colloquial} style, full of slang and half-finished sentences, just as real people talk at the kitchen table.
words.etym: From Latin colloquium, “conversation”: com (together) + loqui (to speak).

mn.text: In class Dev says, “Good afternoon, Professor.” With his pals at the skate park, it’s “Hey, what’s up?” That everyday way of talking is {colloquial}.

scene.alt: Two teen friends greet each other casually at the playground.

words.def: a speech in a play in which a character, alone, speaks thoughts aloud
words.ex: In the second act, the prince delivers a long {soliloquy} about whether to leave home.
words.ctx: The audience learned the villain’s plan through a {soliloquy}: alone on the dark stage, he told no one but himself exactly what he meant to do.
words.etym: From Late Latin soliloquium, “talking to oneself”: solus (alone) + loqui (to speak).
words.note: A soliloquy is spoken alone; a monologue may be spoken to other characters.

mn.cue: SOLO + LOQU: talking ALONE on stage
mn.text: Alone on the empty stage, the prince speaks his worried thoughts out loud to no one at all. His speech is a {soliloquy}.

scene.alt: A young actor dressed as a prince stands alone on stage, speaking his thoughts aloud.

words.def: using many words to avoid saying something directly
words.ex: Asked if he ate the last cookie, Pip answered with ten minutes of {circumlocution}.
words.ctx: The letter was a masterpiece of {circumlocution}: three pages about “adjustments” and “new directions” that never once said the store was closing.
words.etym: From Latin circumlocutio, “a speaking around”: circum (around) + loqui (to speak).

mn.text: Asked if he ate the last cookie, Pip talks about the weather, his homework and the dog, everything except yes or no. That is {circumlocution}.

scene.alt: A mother asks a simple question while her son talks in circles beside an empty cookie plate.

words.def: the skill of pronouncing words clearly when speaking in public
words.ex: Years of {elocution} lessons gave the actor a clear, ringing voice.
words.ctx: In the old one-room schools, {elocution} was a subject of its own; pupils stood before the class to recite poems slowly, loudly and with every consonant crisp.
words.etym: From Latin elocutio, “a speaking out,” from eloqui: e (out) + loqui (to speak).

mn.cue: E-LOCU-TION: speaking OUT, clear as a bell
mn.text: Professor Edwin rings a bell, and Maya repeats the tongue twister until every sound rings out clearly. She is practicing {elocution}.

scene.alt: A professor rings a bell while a teen practices saying a tongue twister clearly.

words.def: the choice of words; also, how clearly words are spoken
words.ex: The poet’s {diction} was simple: short, everyday words that hit hard.
words.ctx: The essay’s ideas were fine, but its {diction} was wrong for a formal letter; words like “stuff” and “a bunch” made the writer sound careless.
words.etym: From Latin dictio, “a saying, a way of speaking,” from dicere (to say).
words.note: On the SAT, diction usually means word choice: a writer’s diction sets the tone.

mn.cue: DICTIONary: choosing the words you SAY
mn.text: Nell flips through her dictionary to pick the perfect word: not “shine” but “glimmer.” Her careful choice of words is her {diction}.

labels.text: DICT = SAY: the words you choose

scene.alt: A writer looks through a dictionary, choosing the perfect word.

words.def: an official order from someone in authority
words.ex: The queen’s {edict} declared every Friday a holiday.
words.ctx: The principal’s new {edict}, posted on every classroom door, banned phones from the cafeteria starting Monday, and no one could argue with it.
words.etym: From Latin edictum, “a proclamation,” from edicere, “to declare”: e (out) + dicere (to say).

mn.text: The royal herald unrolls a scroll and reads the queen’s new order aloud: every Friday is now pie day! That official order is an {edict}.

scene.alt: A herald reads a royal order from a scroll as a girl and a grandfather cheer.

words.def: to formally charge someone with a crime
words.ex: The grand jury voted to {indict} the banker for stealing from his clients.
words.ctx: Because the evidence was strong, the grand jury {indicted} the shop owner, and a trial was set for the spring.
words.etym: From Anglo-French enditer, “to accuse,” from Latin in + dictare (to declare); the c was added later to match the Latin.
words.note: Pronounced in-DITE: the c is silent.

mn.cue: in-DITE: the INVITE no one wants
mn.text: The court’s letter is an invitation nobody wants: it formally charges the thief with stealing the town’s golden goose. To {indict} is to charge someone with a crime.

scene.alt: A judge hands a formal charge to a shocked thief, with a golden goose nearby.

words.def: a person taking part in a conversation
words.ex: Grandpa is a patient {interlocutor}; he lets you finish every sentence.
words.ctx: The reporter was a skilled {interlocutor}: she listened closely, asked one short question at a time and let the long silences do the rest.
words.etym: From Latin interloqui, “to speak between, interrupt”: inter (between) + loqui (to speak).

mn.cue: INTER-LOCU-TOR: the one you speak BETWEEN
mn.text: Across the café table, Lin and Omar trade ideas, each listening and answering in turn. Each is the other’s {interlocutor}.

scene.alt: Two friends sit across a café table, taking turns talking and listening.

after.html: Loquacious (very talkative) and eloquent (speaking beautifully) both come from loqui, but they are not the same: a loquacious person talks a lot; an eloquent one talks well.

items.q: In a play, a character alone on stage speaks her thoughts aloud. This speech is a…
items.why: Soli (alone) + loqu (speak): a soliloquy is spoken alone. A monologue may be spoken to other characters.

items.q: Which is true of a loquacious speaker?
items.why: Loquacious means very talkative. Speaking beautifully is eloquent.

items.q: True or false: the c in indict is pronounced, so it rhymes with “predict.”
items.why: False. Indict is pronounced in-DITE; the c is silent, so it rhymes with “invite.”

items.q: Which word contains a root that means “say,” not “speak”?
items.why: Edict has dict (say). The others have loqu or locut (speak).
